contentHtml:
LifePrint 3D combines artificial intelligence, advanced image processing and 3D printing to transform ultrasound images into keepsakes families can hold, while opening new possibilities for physical models of human anatomy

Medical imaging technologies such as ultrasound, CT and MRI have transformed the diagnosis and understanding of diseases by allowing doctors to visualise internal anatomy. However, medical images are largely viewed on screens, with limited scope for translating them into physical representations that can be examined or held.

Advances in three-dimensional reconstruction and printing are creating possibilities in this area. One emerging application involves converting 3D or 4D ultrasound scans into physical models of an unborn baby’s face and upper body, allowing expectant parents to view a tangible representation based on an existing scan.

Mumbai-based medical technology venture LifePrint 3D, co-founded by radiologists Dr Anand Bherwani, Dr Sandesh Rothe and Dr Sheetal Kabra, has introduced FirstEmbrace in India. The service converts existing 3D or 4D ultrasound scans into personalised, three-dimensional printed models.

Converting ultrasound data into physical models presents several technical challenges. Unlike CT and MRI datasets, ultrasound images can contain noise, shadows and incomplete anatomical boundaries. Fetal movements, variations in image quality and the baby’s position can also affect the accuracy of three-dimensional reconstruction.

Research has examined the potential emotional impact of such models. An independent randomised controlled study published in the Journal of Obstetric, Gynecologic & Neonatal Nursing in 2020, involving 96 expectant mothers, found that women who received 3D-printed models of their unborn babies experienced a greater improvement in maternal-fetal attachment scores than those who received ultrasound images alone. The average improvement was 8.7 points in the 3D-model group, compared to 4.9 points in the ultrasound-only group.

FirstEmbrace uses existing 3D or 4D ultrasound images to create physical representations of an unborn baby’s face and upper body. The process relies on scans already performed for medical purposes and is subject to the treating doctor’s discretion and the radiologist’s assessment of image quality. It does not require additional ultrasound examinations solely for creating the models.

Dr Sandesh Rothe, Radiologist, Co-founder and Partner at LifePrint 3D, said, “For parents, these are moments that stay with a family forever. We want to give them an opportunity to preserve that memory in a completely different way, something they can actually hold. Importantly, we use scans that have already been performed as part of medical care, without encouraging unnecessary ultrasound examinations.”

Dr Sheetal Kabra, Radiologist, Co-founder and Partner at LifePrint 3D, explained the scientific challenges involved: “Every ultrasound scan is different. The baby’s position, surrounding structures, acoustic shadows, and the quality of the acquired images all influence how much detail can be reconstructed. Converting ultrasound data into a physical model is technically very different from simply printing a photograph. It requires careful assessment of the available anatomical information, image processing and three-dimensional reconstruction. Our focus is to preserve the visible features captured in the original scan while being transparent about the limitations of the technology.”

The use of three-dimensional printing in medical imaging also extends to anatomical modelling. LifePrint 3D is developing physical models from suitable CT and MRI datasets, covering structures such as the heart, lungs, airways, liver, kidneys, brain, spine, bones and vascular systems.

Physical anatomical models can help visualise complex structures and may have applications in medical education, anatomical demonstrations and doctor-patient communication. Their use can provide an additional way of understanding anatomical relationships alongside conventional imaging and clinical reports.

Dr Anand Bherwani, Radiologist, Co-founder and Partner at LifePrint 3D, said, “Artificial intelligence and advanced computational technologies are changing what we can do with medical images. What was once technically difficult and required extensive manual processing is gradually becoming more achievable. Our vision is to bring these advances together and make three-dimensional anatomical models more accessible. We are moving towards a future where medical imaging is no longer only about seeing. It is also about touching, understanding and connecting.”

The company’s current anatomical modelling work is focused on education, demonstrations and patient communication.

FirstEmbrace is classified as a non-medical, non-diagnostic personal keepsake. The models do not replace medical imaging, clinical reports, professional interpretation or the judgement of a treating clinician. They are intended to preserve a visual representation and are not meant for medical assessment or decision-making.

The models are restricted to the baby’s face and upper body. The service does not determine, reveal or communicate the sex of the foetus and is intended to operate in accordance with the applicable provisions of the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994 (PC&PNDT Act).
